records.story: Mellow Corn was first made in 1945 by the Medley Distilling Company of Owensboro, Kentucky, and went out under a yellow label bearing the Medley family crest. The label passed through other hands, and in 1993 it came to Heaven Hill of Bardstown, by Heaven Hill's own account as one of several labels in a deal with United Distillers. Heaven Hill changed almost nothing. The label stayed as it was, crest and all, and the whiskey kept to the bonded rule: one distilling season, four years in a bonded warehouse, 100 proof. From the 1970s, in Heaven Hill's telling, it was for decades the one aged corn whiskey sold across the country. Then, as Heaven Hill tells it, bartenders and drinkers found it again, drawn by the loud label and kept by the grain. In 2023 the house showed the same recipe at twenty years old in its Heritage Collection. For a bartender Mellow Corn is the plain lesson in what separates corn whiskey from bourbon: the same grain at the heart of it, but oak that has held whiskey before.

records.story: Georgia Moon takes its name from the moonshiners of corn whiskey, who ran their stills by moonlight because the smoke would give them away by day, as Difford's Guide tells it. Yet the jar is made in Kentucky, not Georgia, by Heaven Hill, the Bardstown house that five brothers of the Shapira family and a group of local investors founded in 1935, filling its first barrel that December. On 7 November 1996 a fire took Heaven Hill's distillery and seven of its rickhouses. In 1999 the house bought the Bernheim distillery in Louisville from United Distillers and Vintners and moved its distilling there, while ageing and bottling stayed near Bardstown. Through all of it Georgia Moon kept its glass mason jar and its wink of a label, less than 30 days old. In 2008 Heaven Hill added two flavoured versions, peach and lemonade, at 70 proof in the same jar. Behind a bar Georgia Moon is the lawful face of moonshine: a corn whiskey, taxed and labelled, that has spent almost no time in wood, and a plain way to show a guest what corn tastes like before the barrel.

records.story: Moonshine in the Tennessee hills was often corn whiskey made out of the taxman's sight and sold clear and young. Even after national Prohibition ended, Tennessee kept lawful distilling within narrow bounds: before 2009 it was allowed in only three counties, Moore, Coffee and Lincoln, the homes of Jack Daniel's, George Dickel and Prichard's. In 2009 the legislature opened distilling to 41 more counties, those that already allowed both liquor stores and liquor by the drink, and Sevier County was among them. Ole Smoky opened in the mountain town of Gatlinburg in 2010, started by a group of local lawyers. It set out to make the hills' own spirit lawfully: corn whiskey, clear and unaged, in a glass jar, from what the house calls a recipe a hundred years old, which is its own claim and not a matter of record. Flavoured jars followed the Original, and more distilleries in Tennessee followed the one in Gatlinburg. For a bartender the Original is the moonshine a guest names, and the plain proof that a lawful jar of moonshine is corn whiskey that never met a barrel.

records.story: Ben Holladay (1819 to 1887) and a brother founded a distillery at a limestone spring in Weston, Missouri, in 1856, and Ben went on to run stagecoach lines across the West as the Stagecoach King. By 1900 the distillery had passed to the Shawhan family and taken their name. The company changed its name more than once in the years that followed, and in 1942 its owners took the McCormick name and the company became McCormick Distilling. Under that name it sent out Platte Valley, a straight corn whiskey in a ceramic jug sealed with a cork. In 2016, for the 160th year of the site, the old distillery took back the Holladay name and turned again to making bourbon of its own. For a bartender Platte Valley is the aged corn in the jug: the bottle that shows a guest that corn whiskey can rest in oak, look like moonshine and yet not be bourbon, and the jug is the part of it a guest remembers.

records.story: Balcones was founded in Waco in 2008, in a former welding shop under a bridge. Distilling began in 2009, and Baby Blue was the whisky it began with, made from roasted blue corn: as Imbibe tells it, the corn began as Hopi blue corn grown in New Mexico, before the house turned to a blue flint corn grown in West Texas. A corn whisky aged in used oak and bottled at 92 proof, it made the name of a distillery that went on to malt, rye and smoked whiskies. In 2014 the founder left after a dispute with the company's investors, and the distillery carried on without him. In 2011 the company bought the old Texas Fireproof Storage building in downtown Waco, a few blocks away, and in 2016, after two years of building work, began distilling there on larger copper stills made by Forsyths of Scotland. The used oak is what keeps Baby Blue a corn whisky and not a bourbon. For a bartender it is the craft answer to Mellow Corn: corn whisky made to be sipped, with the roast of the corn in the glass.
